Day 1

Day 1 — How Markets Actually Work

🎬 The story of 45 minutes that broke Wall Street's brain

On May 6, 2010, at 2:32 PM New York time, the Dow Jones was having a bad but ordinary

day — down about 300 points. Then, in the next 36 minutes, it fell nearly 1,000 points

more. For a few minutes, shares of the consulting firm Accenture traded at one cent.

PG&E — a boring, stable utility — traded at $39,999.99 a share. P&G itself crashed

37% in minutes, then recovered almost everything before the closing bell.

No asteroid hit. No bank collapsed. What happened was simpler and more important:

one large mutual-fund company started selling about $4.1 billion worth of

stock-market bets, all at once, into a market where buyers had quietly stepped away. For a few minutes, there were almost no agreements between buyers and

sellers at any price. So prices — remember, prices are just the last agreement —

printed absurd numbers until buyers returned. The SEC later called it the Flash Crash.

Sit with that: the most sophisticated market on Earth briefly priced Accenture at 1

cent and a power company at $39,999.99. Not because anyone decided those were fair

prices — but because those were the last agreements between the few buyers and sellers

still standing.

That is the entire subject of today's lesson. Once you truly understand what a price

is, 80% of trading confusion evaporates.

💬 Before we start — honest answers only: if you'd had money in the market on March 13, 2020 (the day Nifty froze at the lower circuit), do you think you'd have been one of the people frantically pressing sell… or one of the frozen watchers refreshing the app? There's no wrong answer. Yet. Jot down your guess — by tonight you'll know exactly what you'd have been watching.

What you'll learn

  • - What a "price" actually is (the Flash Crash makes it obvious)
  • - Why prices move up and down
  • - Who you're trading against

    • A market is an auction — nothing more

    Forget the news, the indicators, the opinions. At its core, every market is an auction

    with one item for sale and millions of bidders.

  • - A buyer says: "I'll pay ₹24,100 for one Nifty futures contract."
  • - A seller says: "I'll only sell at ₹24,120."
  • - When a buyer agrees to pay the seller's price (or vice versa), a trade happens —

    • and the price on your screen updates to that last traded price.

    **The price on your screen is simply the price of the most recent agreement between one

    buyer and one seller.** Accenture at ₹0.01 wasn't a valuation — it was the last

    agreement in a temporarily empty room.

    Why prices move

    Prices move for one reason only:

    **When aggressive buyers outnumber aggressive sellers, price rises. When aggressive sellers outnumber aggressive buyers, price falls.**
  • - Aggressive buyer = someone who hits "buy now" and accepts the seller's asking price.
  • - Aggressive seller = someone who hits "sell now" and accepts the buyer's price.

    • If 1,000 people suddenly want to buy and only 200 want to sell at the current price,

    the buyers consume the available sellers. The next sellers demand more. Price rises.

    The Flash Crash was the extreme version: sellers screamed, buyers vanished, and price

    fell off a cliff until new buyers found the prices attractive enough to agree again.

    Who is on the other side of your trade?

    You are never trading against "the market." You're trading against people:

    ParticipantWhat they wantHow it shows up
    Retail traders (like you)Quick profitsSmall, scattered orders
    Institutions (mutual funds, FIIs/DIIs)Fill huge positions over daysSustained one-directional moves
    Market makersEarn the spread, stay flatConstant two-sided quotes
    HedgersProtect existing holdingsPredictable orders at levels

    Beginners imagine they're trading against geniuses. Mostly you're trading against

    patterns of behavior — and behavior repeats. That's why price patterns exist at all.

    📌 Case file: March 2020 — the panic you will live through again

    Between February 19 and March 23, 2020, the S&P 500 fell 34% in 23 trading days —

    the fastest bear market in history. Nifty did the same in lockstep. News readers were

    paralyzed; auction readers saw something simpler: aggressive sellers everywhere, buyers

    only at lower and lower prices. Every day, the last agreement printed lower. Then on

    March 23, buyers stepped back in aggressively — and the same mechanism ran in reverse:

    the S&P rose roughly 50% in five months and made new all-time highs by August.

    No prediction was needed. Only the ability to read who is more aggressive right now —

    the skill this course builds from the ground up.

    🇮🇳 The Indian story: circuits, panic, and the 7,511 bottom

    You lived the Indian version of the Flash Crash. On March 13, 2020, Nifty hit its 10%

    lower circuit within minutes of opening — trading was frozen, and thousands of sell

    orders sat frozen with it. On March 23, it happened again, and Nifty touched **7,511

    intraday — down ~39% in five weeks. India VIX, the fear gauge, spiked past 83**, the

    highest reading anywhere in the world at that time. Same mechanism as May 2010: sellers

    screaming, buyers gone, last agreements printing lower by the minute. Then, on March 24,

    buyers stepped back in aggressively — and Nifty roughly doubled within eight months,

    closing 2020 near 13,982. No prediction needed — just reading who was more aggressive,

    day by day.

    Key takeaways

  • - Price = the most recent agreement between a buyer and a seller. (Flash Crash: 1 cent

    • to $39,999.99 proves it.)

  • - Price moves when one side becomes more aggressive than the other.
  • - You trade against repeating human behavior, not against "the market."

    • Quick check ✅

  • 1. Price on your screen updates when…?
  • 2. If buyers keep "eating" all available sellers at the ask, what happens next?
  • 3. True or false: a big green candle means more people bought than sold at that moment.

    • Today's action step

    Open your charting app, put Nifty 50 on a 5-minute chart, and watch it live for 10 minutes

    (no trading). Don't look for patterns — narrate the auction like a commentator: *"Sellers

    pushing, buyers waiting… buyers stepped in, sellers pulled their orders…"* You're

    training the exact muscle that read March 2020 in real time.

    Day 2

    Day 2 — Brokers & Order Types

    🎬 The 45 minutes that cost $440 million

    On August 1, 2012, Knight Capital — one of the largest market makers in America,

    handling trades for everyday investors — deployed a software update. One line of dead

    code from an old module woke up. Within 45 minutes, Knight's machines had sent

    millions of unintended orders into the stock market, buying high and selling low in a

    loop it couldn't stop. By the time engineers killed it: **$440 million gone — roughly

    $170,000 per second**. Knight's stock collapsed 60%+ and the firm was rescued in a

    fire-sale merger days later.

    Here's why this story opens a lesson for you: Knight's disaster wasn't about analysis.

    It was about the plumbing — what happens between your finger pressing "buy" and the

    exchange matching your order. That plumbing is the broker's world, and you live in it

    every trade. Today you learn the four order types that control exactly how your bid

    enters that auction.

    💬 Quick honesty check: when you open your trading app, do you actually know where your shares are held? If your broker's app vanished tomorrow, could you get your holdings back? Jot your guess in your head — today's two stories will make you want to check. What do you think — safe, or "never thought about it"?

    What you'll learn

  • - What a broker actually does (and Knight's place in the chain)
  • - Market, limit, stop-market and stop-limit orders
  • - Which order type to use when

    • What a broker does

    You can't walk up to the exchange and shout your order. A broker is your licensed

    gateway: your app sends an order → the broker validates and routes it → the exchange

    matches it against another order → the fill comes back to you — all in milliseconds.

    In the chain, your broker also: holds your money, calculates margin, sends contract

    notes, and reports your trades to tax authorities. (And a broker's own systems can fail —

    Knight's did; so can your app's. Choose a broker you trust with money and data. On

    volatile days in India, you've probably seen screenshots of broker outages; the traders

    who planned for it had phone-trade backups. The plumbing matters.)

    The four order types

    1. Market order — "Get me in NOW"

    You accept whatever price is available right now.

  • - ✅ Guaranteed fill, instantly
  • - ❌ No price guarantee — in a fast market you get a worse price (slippage, Day 6).

    • Knight's rogue orders were effectively toxic market orders.

  • - Use when: exiting a losing trade fast. Never for careful entries.

    • 2. Limit order — "Only at my price (or better)"

    You name your price. The order sits in the queue until someone accepts it.

  • - ✅ Guaranteed price (or better)
  • - ❌ Not guaranteed to fill — price may run away without you
  • - Use when: planning an entry at a level you chose in advance. **Your default order

    • type for entries.**

    3. Stop-market order — "If price hits X, get me out NOW"

    Dormant until price touches your trigger, then becomes a market order.

  • - ✅ Your safety net — this is what a stop loss is
  • - ❌ In a panic, fills can be far from the trigger price
  • - Use when: always, on every trade, no exceptions.

    • 4. Stop-limit order — "If price hits X, place a limit at Y"

    Dormant until trigger, then becomes a limit order.

  • - ✅ Price control after the trigger
  • - ❌ Dangerous: in a crash your limit may never fill and you ride the whole fall
  • - Use when: rarely, only once experienced. Beginners skip this.

    Day 3

    Day 3 — Reading Charts: Candles, Timeframes & Volume

    🎬 One tweet, one candle, $365 billion gone

    On May 13, 2021, at 6:06 PM, Elon Musk tweeted that Tesla would stop accepting Bitcoin

    for environmental reasons. Within hours, Bitcoin printed a candle that fell from roughly

    $54,000 to below $46,000 — nearly **$365 billion wiped off crypto's total value in a

    single move**. Six days later, on May 19, a second wave hit: China reiterated its crypto

    ban, and Bitcoin dropped 30% in a day, at one point 50% below its April high.

    If you'd looked at those days on a chart, you wouldn't have needed the news first — the

    candles told you. A giant red body with a long lower wick: sellers slammed price down,

    buyers fought back at the lows. Volume bars three times the normal height: this wasn't

    retail noise, it was a stampede. Today you learn to read exactly that language.

    💬 Try this before reading on: open any chart you have and look at the last candle for five full seconds. Don't scroll, don't analyze. Just look. What do you think it's saying? Hold that guess — by the end of today, you'll read that candle the way you read a headline. Write your first impression in your notes if you like.

    What you'll learn

  • - Anatomy of a candlestick (using the May 2021 dump)
  • - How to read any timeframe
  • - What volume tells you that price hides

    • Anatomy of a candlestick

    A candle compresses four prices from its time period into one picture: Open (start),

    Close (end), High and Low (the extremes). The thick body spans open →

    close; the thin wicks show the high/low excursions.

  • - Bullish candle (green): close above open → buyers won the period
  • - Bearish candle (red): close below open → sellers won the period

    • ✅ Diagram already made: charts/generated/L1-03-candle-anatomy.png

    Read the wicks like a fight replay: on May 19, 2021, Bitcoin's daily candle had a

    massive lower wick — sellers pushed it down ~50% from the April top, and buyers

    rejected those prices so hard that the candle closed far off its low. That long lower

    wick was the first footprint of the bottoming process. A long upper wick is the

    mirror: buyers pushed up and got slapped back. Wicks are footprints of who lost the fight.

    Timeframes: the same movie, different zoom

    A timeframe is just how long each candle represents:

    TimeframeEach candle =Question it answers
    1D (daily)One full day"What's the big picture trend?"
    1HOne hour"Where are institutions active?"
    15m / 5m15 / 5 minutes"Where exactly do I enter?"
    1mOne minuteScalping territory — ignore for now
    Golden rule: the lower the timeframe, the more noise. During the May 2021 crash,

    the daily candle told a clear story of panic-then-defense. The 1-minute chart that

    day was a seizure — thousands of whipsaws that would have triggered and stopped out

    anything mechanical. Same event, different truth, depending on zoom.

    Day 4

    Day 4 — Points, Ticks & Lot Sizes: What a Move Is Worth

    🎬 The day oil went below zero — and destroyed people who never read the contract

    On April 20, 2020, something happened that had never happened in market history: the

    May WTI crude oil futures contract closed at minus $37.63 per barrel. Sellers were

    paying buyers to take oil off their hands. Thousands of traders — many in India trading

    US oil ETFs and contracts through apps — were wiped out. Some owed more than they put in.

    Most of them had never read the contract they were trading. They didn't know what a

    "barrel" unit meant for their P&L, that futures expire and force delivery mechanics,

    that the contract they held was about to roll. They knew "oil is cheap, it must bounce."

    They did not know what one point of oil was worth to them. Today you learn the

    lesson those traders paid their accounts for — it's the least glamorous and most

    profitable lesson in Level 1.

    💬 No scrolling back: one lot of Nifty, and it moves 100 points. What's that in rupees? Take a real guess right now — type it as a reply if you're feeling brave. Most people who've traded for a year get this wrong, and the April 2020 oil traders lost their accounts getting it wrong. That's why today exists.

    What you'll learn

  • - Points vs ticks — and why the WTI crash was a contract-knowledge disaster
  • - Lot size / contract multiplier
  • - Converting a price move into rupees

    • Why this lesson exists

    Ask a beginner: "Nifty moved 50 points — how much did you make?" Most can't answer.

    If you don't know what a move is worth in money before you trade, you're not trading —

    you're the April 20, 2020 crowd, hoping.

    The vocabulary

    TermMeaningExample (Nifty futures)
    PointOne unit of price24,100 → 24,150 = 50 points
    TickSmallest price incrementNifty = 0.05 points
    Lot sizeMinimum quantity per contractNifty futures lot = 75 (check current)
    MultiplierLot size × 1 (for futures)1 point = ₹75 per lot
    Tick valueValue of one tick0.05 × 75 = ₹3.75

    The oil traders' fatal gap: they knew oil's price, not their exposure. WTI's contract is

    1,000 barrels per contract — a $1 move = $1,000 per contract. When oil went from $18 to

    -$37, that was a -$55,000 swing per single contract. Knowing that number beforehand

    is the entire lesson.

    The only formula you need

    Profit/Loss = Points gained × Lot size × Number of lots

    Example: You buy 1 lot of Nifty futures at 24,100 and exit at 24,150.

  • - Points gained = 50 · Lot size = 75 · P/L = 50 × 75 × 1 = ₹3,750 (before charges)

    • Same move in a stock: buy 100 shares at ₹500, sell at ₹510 → ₹10 × 100 = ₹1,000.

    📝 My notes for Day 4

    Day 5

    Day 5 — Leverage & Margin: The Multiplier

    🎬 The ₹2 lakh ticket to an ₹18 lakh position

    Meet Meena. She has ₹2 lakh in her trading account, and she's bullish on the market.

    Without the instrument you're about to learn, participating would be impossible: one

    lot of Nifty futures represents 75 × 24,000 = ₹18 lakh of index. Meena doesn't

    have ₹18 lakh. End of story.

    Except it isn't. Her broker asks for only about ₹1.5–2 lakh as margin — a security

    deposit — and lets her hold the position. That's leverage: the ability to control a

    large position with a small deposit. It's the reason a small account can trade markets

    at all, and it's available to you every single day on NSE.

    Now watch the same tool do two very different jobs.

    Job one — with a plan. Meena buys at 24,100 with a stop at 24,040 (her idea is

    "wrong" below 24,040, plain and simple). Nifty rises 200 points over the next week.

    Her gain: 200 × 75 = ₹15,000 — about 7.5% on her ₹2 lakh account in days. She

    controlled ₹18 lakh with ₹2 lakh, and a planned trade paid her. This is leverage doing

    exactly what it was built for.

    Job two — without a plan. Ravi, same account, same lot — but no stop, because

    "it'll come back." Nifty falls 500 points in a bad week. His loss: 500 × 75 =

    ₹37,500 — nearly 19% of his account, gone. Not because leverage is evil. Because

    Ravi's plan was a feeling.

    Same tool. Same market. The multiplier amplified whatever was attached to it — Meena's

    plan, or Ravi's hope. Leverage is not good or bad. It simply multiplies your process.

    Today you learn to make sure what's attached to it is a plan.

    💬 One word will do: Meena made ₹15,000 in a week on a planned trade. Ravi lost ₹37,500 on hope. Same tool, same market, same month. What do you think the real difference between them was? Prediction? Luck? Personality? Note your one word — then see if it survives today's lesson.

    What you'll learn

  • - What leverage and margin actually are (Meena's version)
  • - How the multiplier works in both directions
  • - The leverage you're actually using — and the two rules that make it safe

    • What is leverage?

    **Leverage lets you control a large position with a small security deposit called margin.** You own the profit or loss of the full position — the margin is just the deposit.

    Meena's example above is 9× leverage (₹18 lakh position ÷ ₹2 lakh margin). Her broker

    holds the margin as security and settles her P&L in cash daily (that's "mark-to-market"

    — profits added, losses deducted, every day).

    How the multiplier works

    Nifty movesAgainst 1 lot (75)On ₹2 lakh marginWith Meena's stop?
    50 points₹3,7501.9%Never reached
    200 points (favor)+₹15,000+7.5%Banked
    500 points (against)₹37,50018.8%Exited at −₹4,500

    See the design: with a stop, the multiplier works for her on good trades and the

    stop caps it on bad ones. Without a stop, there's no cap at all. The tool didn't change

    — the plan did.

    The margin call

    If losses eat into your margin, the broker asks for more money — a margin call.

    Can't add funds? The position is closed for you, at whatever the market gives, usually

    the worst moment. A stop loss you chose beats a margin call the broker chose, every

    time. (Days 18–20 will make your stop and your size automatic.)

    The leverage you're actually using

    Most beginners think: "I don't use leverage, I trade stocks." Check again:

    InstrumentTypical leverageNotes
    Equity delivery (CNC)1×No leverage
    Equity intraday (MIS)3–5×Broker blocks a fraction of value
    Futures5–10×Daily mark-to-market
    Options buyingPremium at riskCan go to zero; max loss = premium paid
    Options selling5–8×Bigger obligations — we'll cover this much later

    Notice: options buying is the only one where the most you can lose is fixed upfront —

    the premium you paid. That's one reason beginners start there.

    The two rules that make leverage safe

  • 1. Every leveraged position carries a stop loss chosen by you, from the first second.

    • (Day 18: placed beyond the structure, not by feeling.)

  • 2. Position size comes from the formula, never from the margin available. The broker

    • will happily let you use all your margin. The formula often says use a quarter of it.

    (Day 20.)

    With those two rules, leverage is what lets a ₹2 lakh account build like a much larger

    one. Without them, the multiplier runs the other way. Same as Meena and Ravi — the tool

    was identical.

    🇮🇳 The Indian story: crores of traders, almost none with these two rules

    India runs one of the world's biggest leveraged retail markets, and SEBI measured the

    result: in its FY22–FY24 study, 93% of individual F&O traders lost money, average

    losses around ₹2 lakh per trader, total retail F&O losses near ₹1.8 lakh crore.

    Read that data carefully, though — it doesn't say leverage lost the money. It says

    traders without a written stop and a calculated size lost the money. The winners in

    SEBI's data used the same leverage, the same products, the same market. The difference

    was never the tool. Over the next fifteen days, you install the two rules above — and

    the same products that drained ₹1.8 lakh crore become usable, on your terms.

    Key takeaways

  • - Leverage = controlling a large position with a small margin deposit. It's the tool that

    • lets small accounts trade big markets at all. (Meena: ₹18 lakh position, ₹2 lakh

    deposit, +7.5% in a planned week.)

  • - The multiplier runs both directions — the stop and the size decide which direction

    • matters to you. Never the broker's margin limit.

  • - Two rules make leverage safe: your stop on every position, size from the formula.

    • Quick check ✅

  • 1. One Nifty lot = ₹18 lakh position on ₹2 lakh margin. Nifty rises 200 points. Gain in

    • ₹, and roughly what % of the margin?

  • 2. What's the difference between a stop loss and a margin call — who chooses each one?
  • 3. Which instrument in the table has its maximum loss fixed upfront?

    • Today's action step

    Open your broker's margin calculator. Type in one Nifty futures trade and one intraday

    stock trade. Write down the margin each blocks, and your implied leverage (position

    value ÷ margin). Then compute: if your stop were hit on each, what % of your account

    would you lose? That last number — not the leverage number — is the only one that

    matters. You're about to learn to control it precisely.

    Answers: 1 — 200 × 75 = ₹15,000 ≈ +7.5% of ₹2 lakh ·

    2 — Stop loss: you choose the exit level before entering. Margin call: the broker forces

    an exit when your deposit runs out · 3 — Options buying (max loss = the premium you paid)

    Day 6

    Day 6 — Long vs Short, Spreads & Slippage

    🎬 The 15 minutes that broke currency brokers

    On January 15, 2015, at 9:30 AM Swiss time, the Swiss National Bank — without warning — cancelled its three-year-old promise to keep the Swiss franc from rising too fast against the euro. In roughly **15

    minutes, the franc surged 30–40%. Within days, Alpari UK was bankrupt** and

    FXCM — the largest US retail forex broker — needed a $225 million emergency loan to

    survive. What killed them wasn't the direction — it was the plumbing: during those

    minutes, bid-ask spreads on EUR/CHF blew from fractions of a pip to several dollars

    wide, and stop losses filled miles from their triggers. Slippage did the rest.

    The SNB shock is the perfect story for today, because it contains all three of our

    subjects: making money in both directions (franc buyers made fortunes that day),

    the spread, and slippage — the two hidden costs that quietly tax every trade you place.

    💬 Have you ever… bought a stock, watched it go UP, and still lost money on the trade? If yes, today's lesson will feel like someone reading your diary. If no — it's coming for you eventually, and the Swiss franc story is why. What's your guess: what invisible thing ate that profit?

    What you'll learn

  • - Going long vs going short
  • - The bid-ask spread (and how it blew out on January 15, 2015)
  • - Slippage — and when it hurts most

    • Long vs short

    Going long = buying first, selling later. Profit when price rises.

    (Buy at 100, sell at 110 → +10.)

    Going short = selling first, buying back later. Profit when price falls.

    (Sell at 100, buy back at 90 → +10.)

    Shorting feels strange to beginners ("how can I sell what I don't own?"), but in futures

    and intraday equity your broker facilitates it — you settle the difference in cash.

    And the franc story shows why it matters: while EUR/CHF longs were being destroyed,

    traders short EUR/CHF — or long CHF — made some of the fastest money in currency history.

    Key insight: long and short are symmetric. Professionals are as comfortable shorting as buying.

    The bid-ask spread

    At any moment there are two prices:

  • - Bid — the highest price a buyer is currently offering
  • - Ask — the lowest price a seller is currently accepting

    • The gap = the spread, and you always pay it: buyers lift the ask, sellers hit the bid.

    Liquid stock (e.g., Reliance)500.00500.05₹0.05 (tiny)
    Illiquid stock100.00101.20₹1.20 (1.2%!)
    EUR/CHF, Jan 15 2015, ~9:31 AM"who knows""who knows"effectively unmeasurable

    On liquid instruments the toll is negligible. On illiquid ones — and in panics — the

    spread alone can exceed your entire expected profit.

    Slippage

    Slippage = the difference between the price you expected and the price you got:

  • - Market orders in fast markets (you take whatever's left in the queue)
  • - Gaps — price jumps over your level between click and fill
  • - News shocks — liquidity vanishes for seconds (the SNB morning)
    • Slippage is usually tiny — until the one day it isn't. Stops don't guarantee prices; they guarantee an exit, at whatever the market gives. On January 15, 2015, many stop losses on CHF pairs filled 10–20% away from their triggers. The stops worked exactly as designed. The design has limits.

    The practical rules

  • 1. Trade liquid instruments only — check average daily volume first.
  • 2. Limit orders for entries (you choose your price).
  • 3. Size positions so a slippy stop hurts, never kills.
  • 4. No new trades into major news events — the SNB taught the world that lesson free of charge.

    Day 7

    Day 7 — The Three Types of Analysis

    🎬 Three men, one housing market, three completely different trades

    In 2005–2007, while Wall Street was printing money on US housing, three very different

    analysts looked at the same market:

    The fundamental analyst — Michael Burry's team at Scion Capital — read thousands of

    mortgage documents, ran the default math, and concluded the loans inside mortgage bonds

    were garbage. They bought insurance against those home-loan bonds failing, and held it for about a year and a half while looking wrong — the trade bled money until it didn't.

    When 2008 came, Scion made roughly $700 million for its investors. His lens:

    "what is this actually worth?"

    The technical analyst didn't need to read a single loan file. By 2007, charts of

    homebuilder stocks, mortgage insurers, and bank indices had broken their multi-year

    uptrends — lower highs, neckline breaks — months before the headlines. The price action

    told you credit was cracking. His lens: "what is price doing right now?"

    The sentiment analyst watched the crowd: in 2006–07, CNBC ran "flip this house"

    segments, taxi drivers discussed condo pre-sales, and mortgage originators handed loans

    to anyone with a pulse. When everyone is bullish and the last skeptic has bought —

    that's not confirmation, that's exhaustion. His lens: "what is everyone feeling?"

    One market, three lenses, three valid edges. Today you learn all three — and which one

    this course is built on.

    💬 Pick one, honestly: three lenses — worth (A), behavior (B), mood (C). Which one have YOU actually been using till now, even accidentally? Most people are quietly shocked when they realize. Note A, B, or C — no judgment, we all start somewhere.

    What you'll learn

  • - Technical, fundamental, and sentiment analysis
  • - What question each one answers
  • - Which style fits which trader

    • 1. Fundamental analysis — "What is it worth?"

    Revenue, profits, debt, management, industry trends, macro. Home country: investors and

    position traders. Strength: catches big moves early, ignores noise. Weakness: *"the market

    can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent"* — Burry's investors nearly pulled

    out before the payoff, because being early looks exactly like being wrong.

    2. Technical analysis — "What is it doing right now?"

    Trends, levels, patterns, volume — no opinions, only behavior. Works on anything liquid

    (Nifty, gold, Bitcoin, USDINR — same rules); gives exact entries, stops, targets.

    Weakness: reads the present, not the future.

    3. Sentiment analysis — "What is everyone feeling?"

    Put-call ratios, open interest shifts, funding rates, news euphoria. Extremes in

    sentiment often mark tops (2007 housing) and bottoms (March 2020, when panic peaked and

    so did the selling). Weakness: hard to time; the crowd can stay greedy for a long time.

    📊 CHART NEEDED: charts/L1-07-three-analyses.png

    INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: One stock · daily · last 6 months

    MUST SHOW (three annotation styles on the SAME chart):

  • - Fundamental: an earnings date + arrow "earnings gap — business repriced"
  • - Technical: trendline + support zone + breakout arrow
  • - Sentiment: at a local top, "news euphoria, everyone's bullish → reversal"

    • Which one do you use?

    **Fundamentals decide what to watch. Sentiment warns when the crowd is extreme. Technicals decide when and where to pull the trigger.**

    Why this course teaches technicals first

    Exact, testable rules (enter here, stop here, target here); works across every liquid

    market; fundamentals can be added later as a filter, sentiment as a warning light.

    🇮🇳 The Indian story: Paytm's listing and Reliance's raise — the same year, opposite lenses

    2021 gave you both lenses in one year. Fundamental: in April–June 2020, while the

    market was crashing, Reliance Industries raised ₹1.52 lakh crore in 58 days selling

    stakes in Jio — investors read the business and paid up even mid-panic. The stock led

    Nifty's recovery. Sentiment: in November 2021, Paytm's IPO listed at ₹1,955 against

    a ₹2,150 issue price and closed −27% on day one, then fell toward ₹500 as IPO euphoria

    — India's own dot-com moment — deflated. Everyone wanted in; the crowd's excitement WAS

    the warning. Same market, same year: one trade from the fundamentals, one lesson from

    the mood.

    Key takeaways

  • - Fundamental = worth · Technical = behavior · Sentiment = mood. (2008 showed all three

    • working in parallel.)

  • - Professionals blend all three; beginners master technicals first.
  • - Every tool answers a different question — confusion comes from asking the wrong tool.

    • Quick check ✅

  • 1. Which analysis type gives you an exact stop-loss level?
  • 2. "The stock is undervalued, I should buy" — which lens? What's its risk?
  • 3. At an extreme bullish sentiment, a contrarian starts thinking about…?

    • Today's action step

    Open the chart of one stock you like. Ask the three questions out loud — What is it

    worth? What is it doing? What is everyone feeling? Notice how each question pulls you

    toward a different decision. That awareness is the lesson.

    Answers: 1 — Technical · 2 — Fundamental; can stay "undervalued" (falling) far longer

    than expected · 3 — Selling/shorting, or at least taking profits

    Day 8

    Day 8 — Find Your Trading Style (Level 1 Finale)

    🎬 The Turtle experiment — proof that style is a system, not a personality

    In 1983, two legendary commodities traders made a bet. Richard Dennis believed great

    traders were made — teachable. His partner Bill Eckhardt believed they were born.

    To settle it, Dennis recruited about 20 people with no trading experience — a

    security guard, a blackjack player, an accountant — gave them a simple mechanical

    trend-following system and strict risk rules, and let them trade real money.

    The "Turtles" went on to earn a reported $175 million+ in aggregate. Here's what

    matters for today's lesson: the Turtle system was a swing/position system. It held

    trades for days to weeks, risked a fixed small fraction per trade, and ignored all

    intraday noise. Dennis deliberately picked the style * beginners could execute without

    losing their minds — not the fastest, not the flashiest, the survivable* one.

    Forty years later, the lesson is unchanged: the best style for you isn't the one that

    makes the most money in theory — it's the one your life and your nervous system can

    execute without breaking. Today you pick yours. Then you take the Level 1 quiz. 🎓

    💬 Gut-check, no thinking: you enter a trade, and ten minutes later your phone shows it's down 3%. What's your honest first move — (a) refresh every two minutes, (b) close the app and check after lunch, or (c) buy more at the "discount"? Note a, b, or c. Your answer matters more than any quiz in this level.

    What you'll learn

  • - The four trading styles
  • - How to choose yours based on time and personality

    StyleHolding periodTime neededStress level
    ScalpingSeconds–minutesFull day, fast reflexes🔴 Extreme
    Day tradingMinutes–hoursMarket hours, focused🟠 High
    Swing tradingDays–weeks30–60 min/day, after close🟡 Medium
    Position tradingWeeks–monthsA few hours per week🟢 Low

    Day 9

    Day 9 — Support & Resistance: Levels That Actually Matter

    🎬 The level that rejected Bitcoin four times — then made the trade of the decade

    Between mid-2019 and mid-2020, Bitcoin ran into roughly the same zone — $10,000 to

    $10,500 — four separate times. Every visit, sellers slammed it back: June 2019

    (pumped to $13,800 on the Libra hype, collapsed), October 2019 (China blockchain speech

    pump, rejected within 48 hours), February 2020 (broke $10k, then COVID destroyed

    everything), and July 2020 (poked above, pulled back one more time).

    Think about what was happening at that zone: every trader on Earth could see $10k. The

    people who bought the June 2019 top and watched -50% were waiting at their breakeven

    to sell. Short sellers who'd won four times expected it to hold again and placed sell

    orders. It wasn't magic — it was unfinished business and remembered pain, stacked

    on top of each other at one price.

    Then, at the end of July 2020, Bitcoin closed above the zone decisively — and over the

    next five months ran from about $10,000 to $42,000. The fifth test wasn't the charm.

    The fifth test was the break — because by then the sellers had spent their ammunition

    across four failed defenses. That's the pattern you'll learn today, and it plays out

    on Nifty every single quarter.

    💬 Ten-second exercise: open any chart right now and find the single most obvious horizontal level — the price your eye lands on first. Found it? Good. Now guess: why is your eye drawn there? Because it's special… or because thousands of other traders' eyes are too? What do you think?

    What you'll learn

  • - Why support and resistance exist (the real reason — the $10k story IS the reason)
  • - How to draw zones instead of lines
  • - How to judge which levels are strong

    • Why S/R exists: market memory

    Every price on your chart is a price where real money changed hands. People remember:

  • - Support = a zone where price fell to before, buyers stepped in, and price rallied.

    • The buyers who missed it return; shorts from higher up buy back there. The zone fills

    with buy orders.

  • - Resistance = the mirror image: a zone where price rallied to before and got

    • rejected. Sellers who missed the exit re-sell there.

    S/R works because of unfinished business and remembered pain — not line-drawing magic. When millions of traders watch the same obvious level, their orders make it real.

    Zones, not lines

    Beginners draw thin lines; professionals draw boxes. Price almost never reverses at an

    exact tick — it reverses within a band, because different participants place orders at

    slightly different prices.

    ✅ Diagram already made: charts/generated/L2-09-sr-zones.png

    (Notice: price touches the zone, not the line — sometimes poking through it briefly

    before reversing. That poke is a "stop hunt," and it's exactly why your zone needs width

    and your stop needs to sit beyond the zone, not inside it.)

    How to mark levels properly

  • 1. Start on the daily chart. Drop to lower timeframes only after the daily map is done.
  • 2. Mark every swing high/low your eye catches in two seconds. If you have to squint,

    • it's not a level.

  • 3. Convert each swing point into a zone covering the wick extremes of the turning area.
  • 4. Mark round numbers — Bitcoin's $10k, Nifty's 24,000, stocks' ₹500/₹1,000. Humans

    • place orders at round numbers instinctively.

  • 5. Mark prior day/week high and low — day traders watch these religiously.
  • 6. Delete everything else. Three to five zones per chart maximum. More lines = more

    • excuses to take bad trades.

    What makes a level strong?

    FactorStrong levelWeak level
    Touches2–4 clean rejections1 touch (untested)
    Rejection styleFast, violent (long wick)Slow drift into it
    TimeframeDaily/weekly levels5-minute levels
    Volume at touchHigh-volume rejectionThin, quiet touch
    AgeRecent (weeks–months)Ancient (years)
    ConfluenceRound number / prior level / MAStands alone

    The paradox: after 4–5 touches, a level gets weaker, not stronger — each visit

    consumes the waiting orders. Bitcoin's $10k died on its fifth test. The level that's

    "held five times" is often one visit from breaking violently.

    Role reversal: the flip

    When support breaks decisively (full body close below the zone, on volume), it very

    often becomes resistance on the retest. Sellers defend their breakeven; new shorts pile

    in. This single concept — trade the flip, not the break — becomes the backbone of your

    pullback entries on Day 22.

    ⚠️ Common beginner mistakes 1. A level at every swing point until the chart looks like a barcode. 2. Trading the first touch — the first approach to a level is information; the trade comes from how price reacts there. 3. Stop loss inside the zone (the stop hunt eats you) — stops go beyond the zone. 4. Moving a "broken" level to make it fit. A level that broke is history.

    Day 10

    Day 10 — Trendlines & Channels

    🎬 The channel that carried oil to $147 — and the line that warned the crash

    From early 2007 to July 2008, crude oil climbed inside one of the cleanest channels in

    commodity history: from around $60 to a peak of $147.27 on July 11, 2008. Along the

    way, every pullback found buyers near the lower rail — roughly three touches — and

    every rally stalled near the upper rail. Traders who simply rode the hallway made

    fortunes while analysts debated peak oil.

    Then the channel broke. Not dramatically at first — just a slide through the lower rail

    in July–August 2008, exactly the "warning, not signal" behavior you'll learn today. By

    December, oil traded near $33 — a −77% collapse in five months. The trendline break

    didn't predict the global financial crisis. It simply told anyone watching that the

    auction had changed hands: buyers no longer defended the lower rail. Months of headlines

    later, the headlines agreed with the line.

    Today you learn to draw that line honestly — and, more importantly, to read its break

    honestly: as a warning, not an alarm.

    💬 Fun one: do you think a trendline works because of geometry… or because of people? Take a side before you read on — reply with your pick. Fair warning: the Sensex's journey from 3,000 to 21,000 has a strong opinion on this.

    What you'll learn

  • - How to define and identify a trend objectively
  • - Drawing trendlines that are actually respected
  • - Using channels to plan entries and exits

    • What is a trend, objectively?

    Strip away the jargon and a trend is just a pattern of swings:

  • - Uptrend = higher highs (HH) + higher lows (HL).
  • - Downtrend = lower lows (LL) + lower highs (LH).
  • - Range = neither — price oscillates between two horizontal zones (yesterday's lesson).
    • "The trend is your friend" is incomplete. The full version: **the trend on your timeframe is your friend.** Oil in 2008 was a monster uptrend on the daily — and a terrifying downtrend by September, on the same chart, in the same year.

    Drawing trendlines without fooling yourself

  • 1. In an uptrend, connect at least two higher lows. Two points define the line;

    • a third touch confirms it. Two touches is a hypothesis, not a level.

  • 2. Connect the wicks — the extremes are where the actual fight happened.
  • 3. Extend it forward. No adjusting to fit more points. If price slices through and your

    • "trendline" looks silly, it was wrong — delete and redraw from the new structure.

    Reading the trendline

  • - Respect = price falls to the line, wicks it, bounces. Trend healthy.
  • - Breaking the line ≠ trend over. A trendline break is a warning, not a signal.

    • What ends a trend is price making its first lower low — structure breaking, not a

    line breaking. Oil's lower rail broke in July 2008; the trend truly ended when rallies

    started failing at lower highs and the August–September swings broke down.

    ⚠️ Common beginner mistake: treating every trendline break as a reversal signal and

    shorting a raging uptrend. The pros fade trendlines maybe 20% of the time; beginners try

    it 80% of the time because it "feels smart."

    Channels: the trend's hallway

    Draw a line parallel to your trendline, anchored at the intervening high (uptrend). Price

    now travels in a hallway:

  • - Lower rail (uptrend) = the buy zone. Pullbacks to it are the highest-probability

    • entries in trending markets (2007–08 oil paid these repeatedly).

  • - Upper rail = the profit-taking zone. First touch in a mature trend = bank partial

    • profits, not add.

    A decisive close outside the channel = the trend is either accelerating (a new,

    steeper channel forms) or ending (like oil, July 2008). You don't know which yet —

    reduce size and let structure tell you.

    Day 11

    Day 11 — Candlestick Patterns: Only the 5 Worth Knowing

    🎬 The hammer that ended the fastest crash in history

    March 23, 2020. The S&P 500 had fallen 34% in 23 trading days — the fastest bear market

    ever recorded, Nifty crashing in lockstep, circuit breakers tripping, headlines

    screaming depression. On that Monday, the S&P printed a daily candle with a long lower

    wick and a small body near the top of its range — in the old language, a hammer.

    Now, here's what separates traders from pattern-collectors: a hammer in the middle of

    nowhere means nothing. This hammer meant something, because it appeared *after an

    extended move (34% down), at a level* (the prior 2018–19 consolidation zone the whole

    world was watching), with panic volume (the highest in history). Buyers hadn't just

    appeared — they had absorbed the largest stampede of sellers in a decade and pushed the

    close well off the lows.

    The next five months: S&P +50%, new all-time highs by August. Nobody knew COVID

    would "resolve." The candle didn't know either. It only reported what the auction did

    that day: sellers exhausted, buyers in control. Today you learn to read those reports —

    and to ignore every pattern that isn't sitting at a level.

    💬 Be really honest: that March 2020 hammer — the candle that ended the fastest crash in history — do you think YOU would have bought it, in real time, while the news was apocalyptic? Note yes or no. Either way, we'll replay exactly what it felt like by the end of today — and you'll see what the buyers saw.

    What you'll learn

  • - The 5 patterns that matter and what each one says
  • - Why context decides whether a pattern works or fails
  • - How to trade a pattern without getting trapped

    • The golden rule of all patterns

    **A pattern at a random location is just a shape. The same pattern at a major level, after a strong move, with a trend behind it is a signal.**

    Before you care about the candle, ask: (1) Are we at a level? (2) Has price

    travelled to get there? The March 2020 hammer passes both tests; a hammer on a quiet

    Tuesday in the middle of a range fails both.

    The 5 patterns that matter

    1. Pin bar (hammer / shooting star)

    One long wick (2–3× the body), tiny body at the opposite end.

  • - Says: price was pushed hard one way and violently rejected — like March 23, 2020.
  • - Trade it: at levels, in the direction of rejection. A hammer at support = buyers

    • defending; a shooting star at resistance = sellers defending.

    2. Engulfing

    A candle whose body completely swallows the previous body, opposite direction.

  • - Says: one side seized complete control of the period.
  • - Trade it: after a pullback within a trend — a bullish engulfing at a rising

    • trendline is one of the cleanest entries that exists.

    3. Inside bar

    A candle entirely inside the previous candle's range.

  • - Says: volatility contraction; a decision is coming.
  • - Trade it: as a breakout trigger — buy the break of the mother candle's high

    • (with the trend). The inside bar itself isn't the signal; its break is.

    4. Doji (at extremes only)

    Open ≈ close; a frozen tug-of-war.

  • - Says: indecision — meaningful only after an extended move or at a major level.

    • A doji after a 12-day rally at resistance is a warning; a doji mid-range is wallpaper.

    5. Morning star / evening star (3-candle)

    Strong candle → tiny stall candle → strong opposite candle.

  • - Says: momentum handover. Rarest of the five, strongest at the right place.

    • Reliability ranking (at a level, with trend)

  • 1. Engulfing at a pullback level
  • 2. Pin bar at a level
  • 3. Morning/evening star at a level
  • 4. Inside-bar breakout (trigger, not standalone)
  • 5. Doji (warning light, not entry)

    • 📊 CHART NEEDED: charts/L2-11-candlestick-patterns.png

    INSTRUMENT / TIMEFRAME: One liquid stock · daily · last 6 months

    MUST SHOW (circle and label all five, each AT a level):

  • - 1 pin bar AT support/resistance
  • - 1 bullish engulfing after a pullback in an uptrend
  • - 1 inside bar with a tradable break
  • - 1 doji at an obvious extreme (aftermath visible)
  • - 1 morning or evening star at a level
    • ⚠️ Common beginner mistakes 1. Trading every pattern instead of every pattern at a level. 2. Entering on the pattern candle itself — the standard play is the break of the signal candle's extreme, stop beyond its other end. 3. Memorizing exotic names (kicking, tasuki, ladder bottom). Nobody's P&L ever depended on a "unique three river bottom."

    🇮🇳 The Indian story: Nifty's own COVID hammer

    You don't have to look at the S&P for the March 2020 lesson — Nifty printed its own.

    After the circuit-frozen panic of March 13 and the 7,511 low on March 23, Nifty's

    candles showed the same signature: panic selling being absorbed. When the government

    announced the nationwide lockdown on March 24 — seemingly the worst possible news —

    Nifty stopped falling and began recovering. The candles were reporting what headlines

    couldn't: the sellers were exhausted, and someone was absorbing everything they threw.

    From 7,511, Nifty added roughly 85% in eight months. Every Indian trader saw those

    candles in real time. Today you know how to read the next ones.

    Key takeaways

  • - Pattern + level + trend = signal (March 2020's hammer had all three).
  • - The 5: pin bar, engulfing, inside bar, doji (extremes only), morning/evening star.
  • - Enter on the break of the signal candle, stop beyond its far end.

    • Quick check ✅

  • 1. Why is a pin bar in the middle of a range worthless?
  • 2. What does an inside bar actually signal, and how do you trade it?
  • 3. Where should the stop go on an engulfing entry?

    • Today's action step

    Open 10 charts. Find one of the 5 patterns at a level on each and write what happened

    in the next 5 candles. Bring the count to 20 over the week — by then you'll feel which

    patterns your market respects, the same way you now know what the March 2020 hammer was

    really saying.

    Answers: 1 — No level = no cluster of orders; random noise ·

    2 — Volatility contraction → trade the break of the mother candle's high/low, with trend ·

    3 — Beyond the far end of the engulfing candle

    Day 12

    Day 12 — Chart Patterns: Double Tops, Triangles, Flags

    🎬 The head & shoulders that announced −78% — while the headlines stayed bullish

    Between March 2000 and September 2001, the Nasdaq Composite built one of the most

    famous structures in chart history: a head and shoulders topping pattern. Left

    shoulder near 5,000 in March 2000. Head — the final blowoff top at **5,132 on March

    10, 2000** (the dot-com peak). Right shoulder through 2001: a lower high near 2,300–2,400,

    visibly weaker. Then the neckline broke.

    Here is what makes this story unforgettable: the news stayed bullish the entire time.

    "New economy." "It's different this time." Analysts were still upgrading internet stocks

    as the neckline gave way. The pattern didn't read the news — it read the *transfer of

    power*: each rally was making a lower high because the buyers of March 2000 were trapped,

    and every bounce was distribution. By October 2002, the Nasdaq traded near 1,114 —

    down 78% from the head. The technicians who trusted the shape were out a year before

    the economists admitted what had happened.

    Today you learn that shape — and its five siblings.

    💬 Trust your eyes first: look at the shape of the Nasdaq 2000–2001 chart in today's story — the rise, the bump, the lower bump, the slide. Without knowing a single rule… does that shape look like something ending to you? Note your raw instinct. Today we give that instinct rules.

    What you'll learn

  • - The 6 chart patterns worth knowing
  • - How to project targets with measured moves
  • - Why volume is the pattern's lie detector

    • Two families

  • - Reversal patterns appear after an extended move and signal exhaustion: double

    • top/bottom, head & shoulders.

  • - Continuation patterns appear mid-trend as the market catches its breath: flags,

    • pennants, triangles. They resolve in the trend's direction more often than not.

    The 6 patterns that matter

    1. Double top (M)

    Two rallies to the same zone, the second weaker, then a break below the middle low

    (the neckline). The crowd that bought the second top is trapped; their exits fuel

    the fall.

    2. Double bottom (W)

    The mirror: two dips to the same zone, the second holds, break above the neckline.

    Trapped shorts fuel the rally. Complete only when the neckline breaks — before that

    it's just two lows.

    3. Head & shoulders / inverse

    Left shoulder → higher head (final euphoria — Nasdaq, March 2000) → lower right shoulder

    (buyers exhausted). Neckline break = confirmation. It works because it visibly maps the

    transfer of power from buyers to sellers.

    4. Bull flag / pennant

    A sharp near-vertical rally (the flagpole) followed by a small downward drift

    (flag) or contraction (pennant). The drift is profit-taking, not reversal. Break of the

    flag's upper edge continues the move.

    5. Symmetrical triangle

    Lower highs + higher lows converging — compression. Trade the breakout either way,

    with volume as the judge.

    6. Ascending/descending triangle

    Flat edge on one side (a real wall of orders), sloping edge on the other. Flats held

    3+ times are powerful; the break of the flat side is often explosive.

    The measured move: how to set targets

    Target = breakout point ± the pattern's height

    Double bottom with 100 points between lows and neckline → target = neckline + 100.

    Flag with a 200-point pole → target = flag break + 200. You don't need to believe it —

    log it over 30 trades and let your own data convince you (Day 28 makes this systematic).

    Volume: the pattern's lie detector

    What you seeWhat it means
    Pattern forming on declining volumeHealthy — sellers drying up / buyers resting in flags
    Neckline break on big volumeConfirmed — trapped side rushing out
    Breakout on weak volumeSuspect — likely a fakeout (Day 22)
    Second top on higher volume with no price progressDistribution — strong hands unloading into excitement. Extra bearish.

    Day 13

    Day 13 — Moving Averages

    🎬 The line that saved investors in 2008 — and the crosses that lie on schedule

    From January 2008 to March 2009, the S&P 500 fell roughly 57%. For almost that entire

    period — over a full year — the index traded below its 200-day moving average, and

    every rally back toward the line was sold. An investor with one rule — "I'm long only

    above the 200-day" — would have sidestepped the worst crash since the Depression, then

    been back in by May 2009 when price reclaimed the line. No prediction. No genius. One

    filter.

    Now the cautionary tale. Fast forward to March 14, 2022: the S&P printed a "death cross"

    (50-day crossing below the 200-day) and financial media ran ominous segments. It sounded

    meaningful — and the market indeed fell further. But flip through history: December 2018's

    death cross came within days of the bottom, and whipsawed bull-market followers. Even

    in 2022, by the time the cross printed, half the decline was already over.

    Same indicator. One use saves you in 2008; the other use fakes you out in 2018. Today

    you learn the difference — and it's the difference between using moving averages and

    being used by them.

    💬 Honest one: in 2008, Nifty stayed below its 200-day average for 17 months. Do you think you could have stayed out that long while everyone around you was "buying the dip" every single month? What would you actually have done — reply with your honest answer, because this test comes for every trader eventually.

    What you'll learn

  • - What a moving average really is (the psychology inside the math)
  • - SMA vs EMA — and why the difference rarely matters
  • - The 20/50/200 framework: filter, dynamic level, pullback entry

    • What a moving average actually is

    A 50-day moving average is the average price of the last 50 days — the average opinion

    of the last 50 days' buyers and sellers. Price above it means the average participant is

    profitable and calm; below it means the average participant is losing and anxious.

    The MA is a map of the crowd's mood and cost basis. In 2008, price below the 200-day

    meant the average buyer of the last year was underwater — every rally met their

    breakeven selling. That's why the line held as resistance for 14 months.

  • - SMA weights all days equally; EMA weights recent days more. For today's uses

    • they behave almost identically — pick EMA and be done.

    The 20 / 50 / 200 framework

    MATimeframeWhat it represents
    20 EMA~1 month of trading daysThe swing trader's line — momentum pulse
    50 EMA~1 quarterThe intermediate trend
    200 EMA/SMA~1 yearThe big trend — bull/bear divide

    These numbers work because everyone uses them — self-fulfilling tools are the best kind.

    Use 1 — The trend filter (the 2008 lesson)

    **Only take longs when price is above the 200 MA on your trading timeframe. Only take shorts when below it.**

    This one filter eliminates the majority of beginner losses, because most losses come

    from fighting the main trend. You will be amazed how much of "skill" is just refusing to

    fight the 200.

    Use 2 — Dynamic support/resistance

    In clean trends, price respects the MA instead of horizontal levels:

  • - Strong uptrends repeatedly bounce off the 20 EMA.
  • - Each touch-and-hold confirms the trend; the day the bounce fails is an early warning —

    • in 2008, the failed retests of the 200-day from below were the tells.

    Use 3 — Pullback entries

    The institutional bread-and-butter:

  • 1. Price above rising 50/200 → uptrend confirmed.
  • 2. Pullback to the 20 EMA stalls.
  • 3. Enter on the first bullish sign at the MA (engulfing, pin bar — yesterday's patterns),

    • stop below the pullback low.

    You bought the average cost of a month of traders in an established uptrend, with a

    level right under your stop. Simple, boring, profitable — the anti-2008.

    Crossovers: understand the lag

    A "golden cross" (50 above 200) sounds magical and arrives months late — the 2009

    golden cross confirmed a recovery that was already +40% off the bottom. Treat crossovers

    as regime confirmations, not entry triggers: they tell you the tide has turned, not

    where to buy today. Entries still come from levels and pullbacks.

    Day 14 — RSI & MACD: The Two Workhorses (and Their Traps)

    🎬 The divergence that called the top of the crypto mania

    Bitcoin made its first major top on April 14, 2021, near $64,800 — the Coinbase

    listing euphoria. It crashed 53% by May, recovered over the summer, and then in November

    made a new all-time high: about $69,000 on November 10, 2021. The headlines were

    ecstatic — new high! The bulls were right all along!

    But look under the hood at the RSI. In April, momentum peaked with price. In November,

    price made a higher high — and RSI made a clearly lower high. The market needed more

    and more buying effort to produce less and less upward progress. Under the surface,

    momentum was dying. That single divergence was the last warning before a bear market

    that took Bitcoin to roughly $15,500 — a −77% decline.

    Meanwhile, remember May 19, 2021? RSI had screamed "oversold" days before the crash

    bottomed — and kept screaming while price fell another 30%. Traders who treated

    "oversold" as a buy signal got run over by a train going downhill.

    Both stories in one asset, within six months. That is today's lesson: indicators don't

    lie — beginners just ask them the wrong questions.

    💬 The trap test: Bitcoin made a brand-new all-time high in November 2021 — higher than ever! If you'd seen only the price chart, what would you have thought? "To the moon" or "something's off"? Note your gut call — then learn what the buyers at the top never saw.

    What you'll learn

  • - What RSI really measures (it is not "overbought/oversold")
  • - MACD as a momentum regime meter
  • - Divergences: the single best use of both

    • RSI — the momentum speedometer

    RSI (14-period) measures the speed and size of recent gains vs recent losses, 0–100.

    The trap: "RSI 70 = sell"

    In a strong uptrend, RSI lives at 60–80 for weeks. In 2020–21, Bitcoin's uptrend

    spent months with RSI pinned "overbought" while price tripled. **Overbought is not a

    sell signal in a trend — it's a feature of one.** The May 2021 "oversold" buyers

    learned the mirror-image lesson.

    The three correct uses

    1. Regime reading (the best one):

  • - Uptrend: RSI dips to 40–50 and turns up = trend healthy = the pullback buying zone.
  • - Downtrend: rallies to 50–60 and roll over = downside healthy.
  • - In uptrends buy the 40–50 dip, don't sell the 70 reading.

    • 2. Divergence (the November 2021 lesson):

    Price makes a new high, RSI makes a lower high → momentum fading. It doesn't time the

    top (nothing does) — it ends your aggression and tightens stops. Then the structure

    break does the timing.

    3. Failure swings (advanced) — note them, master the first two uses first.

    MACD — momentum's center of gravity

    MACD = 12-EMA minus 26-EMA, with a 9-EMA signal; the histogram shows acceleration.

  • 1. Zero line = regime. Above = bullish momentum vote — a second filter beside the

    • 200 MA. Two agreeing filters beat one.

  • 2. Histogram turns = momentum shifts. Histogram shrinking for days while price

    • still rises = momentum leaking out → protect profits (exactly what BTC's histogram

    did into November 2021).

  • 3. Crossovers = the noisy layer, built from averages of averages — lagging. Trust

    • them only at the zero line, with trend.

    The divergence playbook (your #1 takeaway from today)

  • 1. Price makes new high after a long run → check RSI.
  • 2. RSI makes a lower high → note it, tighten trailing stop. Do not short yet.
  • 3. Price breaks its last swing low while RSI stays elevated → confirmation; now the

    • pullback trade is on.

    Divergences warn (November warned). Structure breaks confirm. You trade the confirmation, protected by the warning.

    Day 15

    Day 15 — Fibonacci Basics (Without the Mysticism)

    🎬 The golden ratio and the fastest recovery in market history

    Here's a number that will either impress you or annoy you: after the COVID crash — the

    S&P 500 falling from 3,386 (Feb 19, 2020) to 2,237 (Mar 23, 2020), a −33.9% collapse in

    23 trading days — the recovery stalled almost exactly where Fibonacci mathematics said

    it should. The 61.8% retracement of that crash sat near 2,947. In late May and early

    June 2020, the S&P reached that zone… hesitated… digested for a few weeks… and then broke

    through and never looked back, hitting new all-time highs by August.

    Did the "golden ratio" cause that? Of course not. But here's the honest mechanism, and

    it's more useful than magic: **tens of thousands of funds, algos, and traders all compute

    the same retracement levels on the same obvious swing** — and place orders there. The

    61.8% zone became a dense band of real buy orders simply because everyone was watching

    it. Self-fulfilling levels are still levels.

    Today you learn to use that crowd behavior — correctly anchored, with confluence, and

    zero mysticism.

    💬 Choose your reaction: a ratio from sunflower seeds and snail shells apparently moves stock prices. Is your first instinct (a) fascinating, (b) nonsense, or (c) who cares, show me the money? Note a, b, or c — all three turn out to be partly right, and by the end of today you'll know exactly which part.

    What you'll learn

  • - The retracement tool and the levels that matter
  • - How to draw it correctly (most people draw it wrong)
  • - Using Fibonacci as a zone-confirmation tool, not a prediction tool

    • The tool and the levels

    The Fibonacci retracement measures how much of a move has been "given back" in a

    pullback. Drawn from a swing low to a swing high (in an uptrend):

    LevelNameWhy it matters
    38.2%Shallow retracementStrong trends barely dip here
    50%Halfway backNot even a Fibonacci number — but the crowd watches it
    61.8%The golden ratioThe deepest "healthy" retracement — where the S&P stalled in June 2020
    78.6%The last defenseBeyond this, the move is usually over
    These levels work because everyone uses them. Use them like S/R zones from Day 9 — they ARE popular S/R zones with extra participants.

    Drawing it correctly — where beginners fail

  • 1. Uptrend retracement: anchor at the swing low (start of the move) → drag to the

    • swing high (end). You're measuring the pullback into the up-move.

  • 2. Use the wicks/extremes, not arbitrary candle bodies — the S&P anchor was the

    • March 23 low, the exact panic extreme.

  • 3. Draw on the timeframe of the move you're trading. A daily swing → daily Fibonacci.

    • The golden zone: the 50–61.8% band is where high-quality pullbacks in strong trends

    tend to terminate — deep enough to shake out weak holders, shallow enough to keep

    momentum intact. June 2020 was the world watching that band hold.

    How to actually use it

    Fibonacci's highest value is confluence — it rarely works alone:

  • - Fib 61.8% + prior support zone + 50 EMA = a triple-confirmed buy zone. Take the trade.
  • - Fib 38.2% floating in empty space = a coin flip. Skip it.

    • Simple grading: 2+ independent tools agreeing at one price → A-grade · 1 tool → B-grade,

    half size · Fibonacci alone → no trade.

    For targets, use the mirror — extensions (127.2%, 161.8%): after a breakout,

    project the next leg. Two independent target methods agreeing (extension + measured

    move) is a strong sign.

    Day 16

    Day 16 — Multiple Timeframe Analysis (Level 2 Finale)

    🎬 The day Meta lost $230 billion — and how three timeframes would have read it

    On February 2, 2022, Meta (Facebook) reported earnings after the close: slowing growth,

    heavy metaverse spending. The next morning the stock opened down and closed −26% in

    a single session — about $230 billion of market value, then the largest one-day loss

    in stock-market history.

    Watch that week through three timeframes, the way you will learn today:

  • - Daily (bias): for months before earnings, Meta had been making lower highs from

    • its September 2021 peak — the big picture had already turned down while headlines were

    still warm. The daily said: bearish bias.

  • - 1-hour (setup): into earnings day, the stock was compressed under a clear lower

    • boundary near $320 — a defined level where sellers had repeatedly shown up. The 1H

    said: sell zone identified.

  • - 15-minute (trigger): the next morning's gap-down open, then a failed retest of

    • the prior day's low from below — the first lower-timeframe structure break. The 15m

    said: trigger fired.

    Nobody needed to predict earnings. The top-down process would have had a trader biased

    short for weeks, with a level, waiting for a trigger — and the trigger printed the

    morning after, on the largest one-day collapse in history. That's the power of doing

    things in the right order. Today you install that order.

    💬 Thought experiment: Meta lost $230 billion in one day. In the week before it happened, which chart do you think you'd have been watching — the daily, the hourly, or the 5-minute? Note your pick. Your answer is, quite literally, why this entire lesson exists.

    What you'll learn

  • - The top-down analysis workflow
  • - Why the higher timeframe always wins arguments
  • - How one trade is built across three timeframes

    • The top-down workflow

    StepTimeframeQuestionTools
    1Daily (or 4H)Bias — which direction am I allowed to trade?200 MA, trend structure, major zones
    21H (or 15m)Setup — where exactly is my trade zone?S/R zones, trendline rails, Fib
    315m / 5mTrigger — what candle/pattern gets me in?Day 11's patterns, inside-bar breaks
    The rule that resolves 90% of confusion: the higher timeframe's answer outranks the lower's. Daily says down and your 5-minute chart "looks bullish" (as it did inside Meta on January 31)? The 5-minute chart is noise. Trade with the daily or stand aside — never against it.

    Why lower timeframes lie

    A 5-minute chart contains ~75 candles per day — mostly random auction noise around the

    day's real business. A pattern that "looks perfect" on 5 minutes forms and dies in an

    hour. Meanwhile the daily level it sits on might have three weeks of institutional

    orders behind it — like Meta's $320 boundary.

    Zooming in doesn't add information — it multiplies opinions. Form ONE opinion (on the

    daily) and use small timeframes only for execution precision: cheaper entries, correctly

    placed stops.

    The full trade, built top-down

    Example — long trade (the Nifty version of the Meta story, in reverse):

  • 1. Daily: Nifty above rising 200 MA, pulling back to a major prior-breakout zone.

    • → Bias: long only.

  • 2. 1H: Pullback has retraced into the 50–61.8% Fib band, sitting on the 50 EMA, at

    • the daily zone. RSI curled up from ~45. → Setup: buy zone marked.

  • 3. 15m: An inside bar forms at the zone; you buy its break. Stop below the zone's

    • low. Target: prior daily high / 127.2% extension. → Trigger on. Risk defined.

    One sentence: *"Long Nifty at a triple-confirmed daily zone, in an established uptrend,

    triggered by a 15-minute pattern, risking below structure."* If you can't write your

    trade in one sentence like that, you don't have a trade — you have a feeling.

    The triple-screen rules

  • 1. Maximum three timeframes per trade. More = analysis paralysis.
  • 2. Never trade when timeframes disagree — disagreement means "wait."
  • 3. Risk is defined on the timeframe of your stop (15m trigger, daily stop → size off

    • the daily distance; Day 20 makes this mechanical).

    Day 17

    Day 17 — Entries & Exits: Where the Money Is Actually Made

    🎬 Two traders, one rocket, opposite endings

    In January 2021, GameStop went from about $20 to an intraday high of $483 in three

    weeks. Consider two fictional-but-typical traders who both "saw it early":

    Trader A — the breakout chaser. He watched from $20 to $40, finally bought the

    "momentum breakout" at $120, added at $250 on the second leg, and held for the moon.

    When the squeeze peaked at $483 and reversed, his stops — placed emotionally, based on

    what he needed the stock to do — never triggered where he imagined. He exited most of

    his position around $90, weeks later. He was "right" about the biggest story of the year

    and lost money.

    Trader B — the planned trader. She didn't predict the squeeze; she traded her system.

    She bought the first pullback to a defined level after the initial breakout ($40 zone),

    with a stop below the structure (under $25 — invalidation, not discomfort), and a

    written plan: book half at +2R, trail the rest. She exited most near $300+ and the

    runner on a trailing rule around $200.

    Same stock. Same month. One had an entry style and no exit plan; the other had both.

    The difference wasn't prediction — GameStop was fundamentally unpredictable. The

    difference was that exits, not entries, decided who kept the money. That's today's

    entire lesson.

    💬 The GameStop question: two traders, same rocket of a stock, opposite endings. Before you read a single rule — what do YOU think separated them: better prediction, a better entry price, or better exits? Most people guess wrong, and the wrong guess is why most accounts lose. What's your call?

    What you'll learn

  • - The three entry styles and their tradeoffs
  • - Exit types: target, trailing, time
  • - Why "how you exit" matters more than "how you enter"

    • The three entry styles

    1. Anticipation entry (limit order at the level)

    Place a limit at your zone before confirmation — betting the level holds.

  • - ✅ Best price if right; stop can sit at the ideal structural point.
  • - ❌ Catches falling knives when the level breaks; you get filled because price poked

    • through (the stop-hunt fill).

    2. Confirmation entry (wait for the rejection pattern)

    Price reaches your zone; wait for a pin bar / engulfing (Day 11); enter on its break.

  • - ✅ Higher probability — someone showed you the defense.
  • - ❌ Worse price; fast V-reversals leave you behind.
  • - Beginners should start here — confirmation is training wheels for reading price action.

    • 3. Breakout entry (buy the break of the level/pattern)

    Enter when price closes beyond a boundary.

  • - ✅ Rides momentum; you know fast if you're wrong.
  • - ❌ Worst price of the three; fakeouts are the tax (Day 22).
    • There's no "best" entry — there's the best entry for your psychology. A system you execute calmly beats a theoretically better one you abandon after two losses. (Trader A in our story used a chaotic mix of all three.)

    Exit types — where profits are actually made

    Exit typeHow it worksWhen to use
    Fixed targetExit fully at a predefined level (measured move, extension, prior high)Ranges, clear patterns, when you need predictability
    R-multiple targetExit at +2R or +3R regardless of levelsTrend systems, backtested setups (Day 28)
    Partial + runnerBook half at +2R, trail the restTrends with room — the best of both worlds (Trader B's plan)
    Trailing stopExit only when price reverses X (structure break, MA cross, ATR trail)Strong trends you don't want to cap
    Time exit"If it hasn't moved in N days, I'm out"Everything — dead trades tie up capital and attention

    The two target rules

  • 1. Know your exit before you enter. Exactly — entry, stop, target(s) written down

    • before the order. If you can't name your target, you don't have a trade.

  • 2. Let the structure pay you. First target at the next obstacle (prior high, range

    • edge, measured move). Don't demand 5R in a range that has never given 2R — the chart

    tells you what it pays; your job is to listen.

    A complete example (Day 16's trade, now with exits)

  • - Entry: inside-bar break at the daily zone, 24,100.
  • - Stop: below the zone low, 24,040 (risk = 60 points).
  • - Target 1: prior swing high, 24,220 (+2R) → book half.
  • - Target 2 / trail: 127.2% extension at 24,280, then trail below the 20 EMA.
  • - Time exit: if neither target hits within 5 sessions, exit at market.

    Day 18

    Day 18 — Stop Losses: Placement Rules That Survive

    🎬 The man who moved his stops — and took down a 233-year-old bank

    Nick Leeson was a 28-year-old derivatives trader in Singapore for Barings Bank — the

    UK's oldest merchant bank, founded in 1762, banker to the Queen. In 1994 he began betting that a Japanese stock-market index would stay calm and move sideways. When the Kobe earthquake hit in January 1995, the index crashed right through his comfortable range — and instead

    of taking the controlled loss, Leeson did the thing you're about to learn is forbidden:

    He hid the losing trades in a secret account ("Error Account 88888")… and doubled down, taking bigger positions as the market fell, moving his exits further away, betting on a recovery that kept not coming. The losses snowballed from ~£20 million to

    £827 million. Barings — two centuries of history — was bankrupt within weeks, sold

    to ING for £1.

    The fascinating part: Leeson's initial trades weren't crazy. Selling premium on a

    range-bound index was a standard strategy. What destroyed a 233-year-old institution

    wasn't the entry — it was refusing to define invalidation, then moving the exit to avoid

    realizing pain. Today you learn the discipline that would have saved Barings: where

    "wrong" actually lives on a chart, written before the trade.

    💬 Answer this honestly: in your last losing trade, did you know exactly where you were wrong before you entered — down to the price — or did you figure it out somewhere in the middle of the loss growing? Note "before" or "during." No shame either way. Today makes sure it's always "before."

    What you'll learn

  • - The three valid stop placement methods
  • - Volatility-based stops (ATR) and when structure is ambiguous
  • - The four stop sins that destroy accounts

    • Method 1 — Beyond structure (the default)

    Your stop goes where the idea is invalidated — and ideas live at structure:

  • - Long at support/zone/trendline: stop below the zone's low — beyond where the

    • stop-hunt pokes. If price trades through the whole zone, the defense failed; you're out.

  • - Long at a pullback to the 20 EMA: stop below the pullback's swing low.
  • - Breakout long: stop back inside the pattern, beyond the opposite boundary.

    • Common thread: the stop belongs on the far side of the thing you traded, plus a buffer

    (0.25–0.5× ATR(14) is a sane default) — the buffer absorbs the stop-hunt poke from Day 9.

    Method 2 — Volatility stops (ATR)

    When structure is messy — ranges, fast markets — use the market's own noise level:

    Stop distance = 1.5–2 × ATR(14) from entry.

    If normal noise is 40 points, a 15-point stop is a donation to randomness. ATR also

    scales targets: a 1× ATR target inside a 2× ATR noise market is a coin flip.

    Method 3 — Time-based invalidation

    Some ideas expire: "if it doesn't break out within 3 days, the momentum is gone."

    Exiting on time avoids slow-motion losses where price bleeds theta, attention, and

    opportunity.

    Position size comes FROM the stop — not before it

    The sequence (most people get this backwards):

  • 1. Entry level (from your setup).
  • 2. Invalidation level (structure/ATR) → risk per unit.
  • 3. Risk in rupees (Day 19's 1–2% rule).
  • 4. Size = risk ₹ ÷ stop distance in ₹ per unit. (Day 20 does this math in full.)

    • A wide stop doesn't mean a big loss — it means a smaller size, same rupee risk.

    The four stop sins

  • 1. No stop at all. One gap ends the conversation — this is how Barings died. Every

    • position has a live stop from the first second.

  • 2. Stop inside the noise. Too tight = normal breathing stops you out, then price goes

    • your way without you. The most painful loss in trading: right idea, no position.

  • 3. Moving the stop away. Never. Only toward the target (trailing). Leeson's entire

    • catastrophe is this sin, repeated with size.

  • 4. Instant revenge re-entry after a stop-out at the same level. If the idea still

    • stands, wait for a new trigger (a fresh rejection). One re-entry maximum, then the

    level is dead for the day.
